name: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies

clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant neuropathy caused by a deletion of the PMP22 gene, the reciprocal of the duplication that causes CMT1A
Presents with recurrent, painless, focal motor and sensory palsies precipitated by minor compression, traction or repetitive movement at common entrapment sites
Typical episodes include peroneal palsy with foot drop after leg crossing, ulnar palsy at the elbow, and carpal tunnel-type median symptoms
Deficits usually recover over days to months, though some residual dysfunction can accumulate with repeated attacks
Nerve conduction studies show focal slowing and conduction block at entrapment sites superimposed on a mild, diffuse, often subclinical demyelinating neuropathy with prolonged distal latencies
Nerve biopsy classically shows tomaculous (sausage-shaped) focal thickenings of the myelin sheath
Patients should be advised to avoid prolonged pressure, repetitive strain and positions that compress vulnerable nerves
reference.pathophysiology: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies is caused by a heterozygous deletion of the chromosome 17 region containing PMP22, producing underexpression of peripheral myelin protein 22. Reduced PMP22 renders the myelin sheath structurally abnormal and unusually vulnerable to mechanical stress, so that ordinary compression or stretch at entrapment sites causes focal conduction block and demyelination. Histologically this appears as focal sausage-like myelin thickenings (tomacula). A mild generalised demyelinating neuropathy is often present between episodes, and most acute focal deficits remit as myelin repairs.
additionalDifferentials: Ordinary compressive mononeuropathies (e.g. isolated carpal tunnel or peroneal palsy)
Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies showing focal slowing/conduction block at entrapment sites on a background of mild diffuse demyelination
Genetic testing for the PMP22 deletion, which is confirmatory
Electromyography to assess any secondary denervation
Detailed history of the relationship between deficits and compression or repetitive activity
Family evaluation for autosomal dominant inheritance
Nerve biopsy only rarely, where tomacula may be demonstrated
redFlags: Failure of an expected deficit to recover, suggesting an alternative or additional diagnosis
Progressive, symmetrical or severe weakness atypical for HNPP
Systemic features suggesting vasculitic mononeuritis multiplex
Rapidly evolving generalised weakness raising concern for an inflammatory neuropathy
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally good, with most episodes resolving spontaneously and life expectancy unaffected; however, repeated palsies can leave cumulative deficits, so preventive advice about avoiding nerve compression is important.
pitfalls: Treating recurrent focal palsies as unrelated isolated entrapments and missing the unifying hereditary diagnosis
Failing to counsel patients to avoid habitual nerve compression and repetitive strain
Overlooking the mild background demyelinating neuropathy on nerve conduction studies
Confusing HNPP with an inflammatory neuropathy and giving unnecessary immunotherapy
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
OMIM: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies (PMP22)
